Attempt each question before opening the answers. These questions cover chart
choice, honest visual encoding, prediction workflows, metrics, and leakage.

## Questions

### 1. Chart choice

Which chart is usually most appropriate for showing a numeric value changing
over ordered months?

A. Line chart  
B. Pie chart with 30 slices  
C. Random scatter plot with no x-axis  
D. A table with no labels

### 2. Bar-chart axes

Why should a bar chart comparing magnitudes usually start its value axis at zero?

A. To preserve the visual meaning of bar length  
B. Because all data values are zero-based  
C. To make every difference look larger  
D. Because line charts require it

### 3. Feature and target roles

In supervised learning, what is the target?

A. An input variable used to make a prediction  
B. The outcome the model is trained to predict  
C. A random seed  
D. The test-set row count

### 4. Test-set use

When should the held-out test set be used?

A. Repeatedly while tuning every model setting  
B. For the final estimate after model choices are complete  
C. To fit preprocessing parameters before splitting  
D. Instead of training data

### 5. Classification metrics

When a positive prediction triggers an expensive investigation, which metric asks
how often predicted positives are actually positive?

A. Recall  
B. Precision  
C. Accuracy only  
D. Mean absolute error

### 6. Leakage

Which workflow risks test-set leakage?

A. Fit an imputer inside a pipeline on training folds  
B. Split first, then fit a scaler on training data only  
C. Standardise the full dataset before splitting into train and test  
D. Evaluate predictions on rows not used for fitting

### 7. Grouped data

If several measurements come from the same person, why might a random row-level
split be inappropriate?

A. It can put related observations in both sets, making performance optimistic  
B. It always removes the target column  
C. It prevents any model from fitting  
D. It guarantees perfect generalisation

## Answers and explanations

<details>
<summary>Open answers</summary>

1. **A.** A line chart connects values across an ordered variable, making change
   over time easy to inspect.
2. **A.** Bar length encodes magnitude, so a truncated baseline can exaggerate
   differences between categories.
3. **B.** The target is the known outcome used during training and the outcome
   the model predicts for new cases.
4. **B.** Keep the test set untouched while selecting and tuning models; use it
   for a final estimate after those choices are finished.
5. **B.** Precision is the proportion of predicted positives that are actually
   positive. Recall instead asks how many actual positives were found.
6. **C.** Standardising the full dataset allows test-set information to influence
   the transformation learned before the split, making evaluation optimistic.
7. **A.** Related measurements can let the model recognise the person rather
   than generalise to new people. Group-aware splitting avoids that leakage.

</details>
